name: Opus-fleet deep value
strategy: Concentrated in sub-market-multiple, FCF-rich dividend payers (banks below book, energy, pharma, telecom, staples) with a small hedge shorting the most stretched growth cohort.

positions.thesis: Still my top conviction and unchanged from two sessions ago. 8.73x forward earnings against a 19.11x industry and its own 9.31x five-year mean, a ~6.8% dividend yield, and a price ~13% below its $28.75 peak - the only line I own that never joined the rally, which is precisely why it carries no AI-capex duration and minimal rate duration. That mattered less this week than I expected because the AI trade rebounded, but it is exactly what makes the position robust to whichever way the capex argument resolves next. Q2 lands 8/4 pre-market with consensus at $0.68 on $14.45bn; the company has beaten in each of the last four quarters by an average of ~22% and screens with a positive earnings ESP. Holding the full 18% into the print rather than trading around it - the -18% stop is wide enough to absorb a bad gap without converting a valuation thesis into a stop-out.

Raised from 13% on information that post-dates my fill. Chevron reported Q2 after the 7/31 close: adjusted $6.06 against $5.11 consensus, a 19% beat, revenue $67bn versus $44.4bn a year ago, worldwide production up 20% on legacy Hess assets and the Permian, record US production and record US refinery crude throughput, a 20-year power agreement with Microsoft for a West Texas data centre, and a $1.78 quarterly dividend declared. My entry mark contains none of that. The macro leg is intact and stronger: Brent around $88-90, up more than 20% on the month, with Iran attacking tankers in the Strait of Hormuz. This is the mandate's energy sleeve doing double duty - a sub-market-multiple FCF payer that also hedges the inflation path a Fed pricing a September hike is worried about. Still preferred to ConocoPhillips, whose 42% Kirkuk stake turns an Iran-Iraq escalation into asset risk rather than a tailwind.

Held flat, with a correction to my own record. I previously claimed roughly 0.8x tangible book and buybacks below book; TBVPS is $100.89 against a $132.71 close, so the multiple is ~1.32x tangible and the below-book accretion argument does not hold. What does hold: still the cheapest large-cap US bank at ~11x forward, Q2 delivered $5.8bn of net income on $24.77bn of revenue with ROTCE up to 13%, consensus sits near $155 against $132.71, and the curve has steepened to roughly 100bp (30y 5.28% versus 2y 4.28%) with about two-thirds odds of a September hike priced - a direct net interest margin tailwind. But it has already recovered 4.5% from the no-news sector flush at $127 that I bought, so that specific dislocation is largely harvested. Cheap enough to own at 15%, not cheap enough to size up on a premise I just found to be wrong. Wide stop because the September hike debate will keep the group volatile.

Unchanged; nothing company-specific happened in two sessions. 9.3x forward earnings, a ~6% dividend covered by free cash flow, beta 0.24, a 2026 buyback target raised to $4.5bn, and a $1bn+ dark-fiber deal with Google that makes the AI buildout pay it rent instead of costing it multiple - a structure that looks better, not worse, now that hyperscaler capex has been confirmed at roughly $650bn for the year. The honest headwind is duration: with the 30-year at 5.28% a 6% bond-proxy yield is a thinner spread than it was, which is exactly why this is 12% and not larger. Short-duration contracted cash flows still clear the curve with equity upside, and it compounds in a flat tape.

Held at the trimmed size. The Q2 blowout I was waiting on arrived on 7/30 - $12.54 adjusted against $10.22 consensus, a 27% surprise, revenue $44.5bn against $39.4bn, refining operating income $4.5bn versus $1.3bn a year ago, renewable diesel swinging to $717m of operating income from a loss, and $2.6bn returned at a 59% payout - but my fill was at the 7/31 close, so that print is already in my entry price and is not a reason to add. Best-in-class refining at roughly 8.25x forward with heavy buybacks and Middle East disruption historically bullish for distillate cracks, offset by a position near its 52-week high after tripling and by a crude spike that squeezes feedstock before cracks catch up. Right-sized already; the +20% take-profit harvests a crack blowout without my having to time it.

Unchanged residual ballast. A 13.1x forward, ~5.7%-yielding cash machine with pricing power and a 55-year dividend record, and near-zero beta that is genuinely useful precisely because I am cutting my hedge and adding net long exposure this week. But the deep-value case is thin at these levels - it trades close to its 52-week high and the analyst consensus target sits below spot - and a 5.7% bond proxy is the wrong duration against a 5.28% 30-year with a hike being priced for September. Small enough that it earns carry and dampens the book without my paying up for a discount that has already closed.

Cut from 18% back to the mandate's small structural hedge because the specific catalyst I named has been falsified. I sized this up on hyperscaler capex doubt and SK Hynix's guidance miss; within 48 hours Microsoft showed a $37bn AI business growing 123% with Azure accelerating, Amazon's cloud beat with revenue up 20%, Big Tech capex is tracking ~$650bn for 2026, and SK Hynix and Samsung both posted record single-day gains while SOXX rose over 8%, Micron 18% and AMD 13%. Semis are the direct recipients of the spend that was just confirmed, and the tape is now discriminating between spenders and beneficiaries rather than de-rating duration wholesale. What remains of my case is only that the cohort is up roughly 80% over twelve months and sits below a $671.83 peak while the 30-year yields 5.28% - enough to justify a hedge, not a bet. I keep 6% because the mandate calls for a small short in the most stretched growth cohort and, having checked, SMH is still that cohort: ARKK is flat over twelve months and would be a strictly worse vehicle. Borrow is 3% with no funding cost on shorts, so carry is trivial, and the -22% stop now risks only about 1.3% of NAV.

reassessment_note: Weekly desk 2026-08-01: I got the biggest thing wrong and the cost of admitting it one session in is about 0.2bp, so I am admitting it. My 18% SMH short was explicitly justified by a live catalyst - hyperscaler capex doubt plus SK Hynix's guidance miss - and that catalyst did not fade, it inverted: Microsoft's AI business grew 123% with Azure accelerating, Amazon's cloud beat, Big Tech capex is tracking ~$650bn for 2026, and SK Hynix and Samsung printed their best days on record. That is a demand confirmation for the exact cohort I am short, not sentiment noise, and the split reaction - Meta -8% for refusing a capex outlook on the same day MSFT had its best session since 2008 - shows a market discriminating between AI spenders and AI beneficiaries rather than de-rating duration wholesale, with semis on the receiving end of the spend. What survives is only the weak half of my case, 'it went up 80% so it must fall', which is not an edge and has bankrupted better shorts than me. So the hedge goes back to the mandate's own word - SMALL - at 6%, exactly where it stood before I tripled it. I am not flipping to long semis and I am not switching vehicles: I checked ARKK and it is flat over twelve months, so it is not stretched and would be a worse short. I add 3 points to CVX because genuinely new information landed after my fill - Chevron reported adjusted $6.06 against $5.11 consensus, a 19% beat, with production up 20%, record US output, Hess synergies and a fresh dividend, none of which is in my mark, against Brent up over 20% on the month with tankers being hit in Hormuz. I deliberately do NOT add to Citigroup despite the steeper curve, because in re-checking it I found my own prior thesis was wrong: TBVPS is $100.89 against a $132.71 close, so C trades at ~1.32x tangible book, not the ~0.8x I claimed, and the below-book-buyback accretion argument does not hold; it has also already bounced 4.5% off the flush I bought. Still cheap at 11x with 13% ROTCE, so I hold it, but I will not size up on a premise I have just disproved. The remaining 9 points go to cash at 4%, deliberately: cutting a 12-point short is itself a large increase in net long exposure, from about 54% to about 69%, and I do not want to take that step up in directionality into a Fed with two-thirds odds of a September hike, a 5.28% 30-year, and a live Strait of Hormuz conflict. PFE, VZ, VLO and MO are untouched - nothing about their theses changed in two sessions, and PFE's 8/4 print is a reason to sit still rather than trade.
novelty: I manage no Round-2 book, so there is no same-direction overlap to breach; what distinguishes this book is that it is long the cash-generative, non-duration value cohort - pharma near its 52-week low, a bank at 11x, integrated oil and refining into a Hormuz supply shock, and telecom - while carrying only a token short in the cohort that has just demonstrated its earnings, rather than a large directional bet against AI.
research_notes: Checked the two sessions since my 7/30 rebalance (book filled 7/31 close). (1) The AI-capex de-rating catalyst reversed hard: Microsoft reported Azure acceleration and a $37bn AI business +123%, posting its best day since 2008 (+15-16%, ~$450bn of market cap added); Amazon beat on cloud with revenue +20% y/y to $200.6bn and rose ~9% after hours; Big Tech 2026 capex is tracking ~$650bn. SK Hynix closed ~+30% and Samsung ~+27%, both record days, versus the guidance disappointment I had cited as my live catalyst 48h earlier. SOXX +8%, Micron +18%, AMD +13%. SMH went $504.22 (7/29) -> $538.21 (7/30) and added another leg 7/31. S&P closed 7/31 at 7,489.72 (+0.7%), Nasdaq +1%, Dow +0.53% to 52,485 and a fourth straight winning month, though the Nasdaq-100 still lost ~7% over July. The tape discriminated rather than de-rated: Meta fell 8% for refusing a capex outlook while MSFT soared - the market is paying for demonstrated AI returns, and semis are the direct recipients of that spend. (2) Chevron reported Q2 after the 7/31 close: adjusted $6.06 vs $5.11 consensus (+19%), revenue $67bn vs $44.4bn a year ago, worldwide production +20% on Hess and the Permian, record US output and record US refinery throughput, a 20-year Microsoft data-centre power deal, $1.78 quarterly dividend declared. My entry mark does not contain this print. (3) Energy backdrop intact to stronger: Brent ~$88-90, +20%+ on the month, Iran attacked two tankers in the Strait of Hormuz. (4) Rates: 10y finished 7/31 at 4.75%, 30y at 5.28%, 2y at 4.28% - roughly a 100bp curve - with markets still pricing ~2/3 odds of a September hike under Warsh. Steeper curve helps bank NIM and stays a headwind for bond proxies. (5) Citigroup closed $132.71, up ~4.5% from the $127 flush I bought. Q2 net income $5.8bn, revenue $24.77bn, ROTCE 13%, TBVPS $100.89 - which puts C at ~1.32x tangible book, NOT the ~0.8x I asserted in my prior thesis. That is a factual error I am correcting. (6) Pfizer reports 8/4 pre-market: consensus $0.68 (-12.8% y/y) on $14.45bn (-1.4%), 8.73x forward vs 19.11 industry, ~13% below its $28.75 peak, four straight beats averaging +21.9% surprise, +5.3% over the past month against the S&P's -1.5%. (7) Valero's 7/30 print was a blowout ($12.54 vs $10.22, refining operating income $4.5bn vs $1.3bn, renewable diesel swinging to +$717m, $2.6bn returned) but my fill was at the 7/31 close so it is already in my entry price. (8) Checked ARKK as an alternative hedge vehicle and rejected it - roughly flat to -1.4% over twelve months, so it is not a stretched cohort and would be a worse short than what I hold.
